'''Robert Coleman Richardson''' (June 26, 1937 &ndash; February 19, 2013)<ref name="NobelBio">{{cite web | url = https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1996/richardson/facts/ | title = Biography | work = Nobel Foundation}}</ref> was an American [[Experimental physics|experimental physicist]] whose area of research included [[Orders of magnitude (temperature)|sub-millikelvin]] [[temperature]] studies of [[helium-3]]. Richardson, along with [[David Lee (physicist)|David Lee]], as senior researchers, and then graduate student [[Douglas Osheroff]], shared the 1996 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] for their 1972 discovery of the property of [[superfluid]]ity in helium-3 atoms in the [[Cornell University]] Laboratory of Atomic and Solid State Physics.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last = Osheroff |first = DD
 |author2=RC Richardson |author3=DM Lee
 |year = 1972
 |title = Evidence for a New Phase of Solid He3
 |journal = [[Physical Review Letters]]
 |volume = 28 |issue = 14 |pages = 885–888
 |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.28.885
 |bibcode=1972PhRvL..28..885O
 |doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>
{{cite journal
|last = Osheroff |first = DD
|author2=WJ Gully |author3=RC Richardson |author4=DM Lee
|title = New Magnetic Phenomena in Liquid He3 below 3mK
|journal = [[Physical Review Letters]]
|volume = 29 |issue = 14 |pages = 920–923
|doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.29.920
|year=1972
|bibcode=1972PhRvL..29..920O
}}</ref><ref>
{{cite web

 |title = The Nobel Prize in Physics 1996
 |work = The Nobel Prize in Physics
 |publisher = Nobel Foundation
 |year = 2007
 |url = http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1996/index.html
 |access-date = 2007-08-05
}}</ref>

Richardson was born in [[Washington D.C.]] He went to high school at [[Washington-Lee High School|Washington-Lee]] in [[Arlington, Virginia]]. He later described Washington-Lee's biology and physics courses as "very old-fashioned" for the time. "The idea of 'advanced placement' had not yet been invented," he wrote in his Nobel Prize autobiography. He took his first calculus course when he was a sophomore in college.<ref name="nytprint">{{cite news| last = Chang | first = Kenneth | date = 2013-02-22 | title = Robert C. Richardson, 75, Laureate in Physics, Dies | work = The New York Times | page = B14}}</ref>

Richardson attended [[Virginia Tech]] and received a B.S. in 1958 and a M.S. in 1960. He received his PhD from [[Duke University]] in 1966.

==Background==
At the time of his death, he was the Floyd Newman Professor of Physics at [[Cornell University]], although he no longer operated a laboratory. From 1998 to 2007 he served as Cornell's vice provost for research, and from 2007 to 2009 was senior science adviser to the president and provost. His past experimental work focused on using [[Nuclear Magnetic Resonance]] to study the quantum properties of liquids and solids at extremely low temperatures.

Richardson was an [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]], and mentioned the Scouting activities of his youth in the biography he submitted to the Nobel Foundation at the time of his award.<ref name="NobelBio"/>

Richardson claimed that he did not believe in an [[Personal god|anthropomorphic God]], but it is unclear what specific beliefs he held.<ref>{{cite web | year =2011 | title = 50 Renowned Academics Speaking About God | website = [[YouTube]] | volume = Part 1 | access-date = 2016-09-04 | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s47ArcQL-XQ | quote = But, I do not believe in an anthropomorphic god... | editor = Jonathan Pararajasingham}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Richardson was born to Lois Price Richardson, who attained a Master’s Degree of her own before she met and married Richardson’s father, Robert Franklin Richardson, a [[Telecommunications engineering|telephone engineer]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=22 Feb 2013 |title=Robert Richardson: Physicist who won a Nobel Prize for elucidating the very strange properties of superfluid helium-3 |language=en |pages=33 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/754517969 |url-access=subscription |access-date=3 Jun 2023}}</ref> He married Betty Marilyn McCarthy, a fellow physics PhD student from Duke, on 29 Sep 1962 at the Immaculate Conception Catholic church in [[Durham, North Carolina]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=24 Sep 1962 |title=Couple to Wed this Saturday Feted at Party |language=en |pages=6 |work=[[The Herald-Sun (Durham, North Carolina)|The Herald-Sun]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/791528362 |url-access=subscription |access-date=3 Jun 2023}}</ref> Together they had two children, Jennifer and Pamela; and four grandchildren Jade, Vanessa, Oliver, and Quinn.
